initial_requirements: Project ZNIX aims to provide an object-based, application-independent framework for retrieving and manipulating personal information. Casual users should be able to archive diverse information, organize it through relationships and hierarchies they find meaningful, and add, change, remove, categorize, or back up items without disrupting that organization. The framework should also expose services that allow compatible client applications to work with the same information.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll help gather detailed information about the ZNIX Information Management Framework so we can understand the needs clearly and avoid missing important requirements. Before we begin, are you aligned with this interview scope, or do you expect us to cover something different?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, I’m aligned with that scope. We’re mainly looking at how people store, organize, modify, and back up personal information in ZNIX, and how other applications can use the same information through the framework. If we need to go beyond that into implementation details, we can decide that as we go, but the core focus is on the information management capabilities.

turns.interviewer_utterance: To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?
turns.interviewee_utterance: I’m representing the stakeholder side for ZNIX, with a focus on how the framework should support everyday users and compatible client applications. My concern is making sure the system is flexible enough for people to organize personal information in ways that make sense to them, without locking them into a rigid structure.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Thank you. Could you describe the current process or system people use today for storing and organizing their personal information?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Right now, people tend to use a mix of tools, like file folders, notes apps, email, cloud drives, and sometimes separate databases or document managers. The problem is that the information ends up scattered, and once they organize it one way, it’s hard to reuse that same organization across different apps or keep it intact when things change. Some people also end up copying the same item into multiple places, which creates inconsistency and makes backups and updates more painful.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current processes do you want ZNIX to change or improve, or what core features do you hope to get from this project?
turns.interviewee_utterance: We want ZNIX to replace the scattered, app-specific way people manage information with one shared framework where the data itself stays consistent and usable across tools. The biggest improvement should be that users can reorganize, update, or back up items without losing the relationships and structure they’ve already built. We also want applications to be able to work with the same underlying information instead of each keeping its own separate copy.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Based on your description, should ZNIX also include a way for users to define custom relationships and hierarchies between items, so they can organize information in their own meaningful structure?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, definitely. That’s a central part of it, because different users will think about their information differently, and we don’t want to force one fixed folder model on everyone. They should be able to create relationships and groupings that match their own way of understanding the information.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Are there any other core features you would like to see in this project, beyond custom relationships and hierarchies?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, I’d expect basic item management to be solid as well, like adding, editing, deleting, categorizing, and searching information quickly. Backup and restore are also important, because users need confidence that their organization and content can be preserved. If possible, I’d also want the framework to expose a clean interface so client applications can integrate without having to know too much about how the data is stored internally.

turns.interviewer_utterance: So these are the main features/functions you want to have: shared information storage across applications, custom relationships and hierarchies, basic item management like add/edit/delete/categorize/search, backup and restore, and a clean integration interface for client applications, right?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, that’s right. Those are the main things I’d want ZNIX to provide, at least from the user and integration side.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Which of those main features should be the highest priority to deliver first?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The highest priority should be the shared information storage with stable item management, so users can add, edit, delete, and retrieve information without breaking anything else. Right after that, I’d put custom relationships and hierarchies, because that’s what makes the system genuinely useful instead of just another storage layer. Backup and the client integration interface are also important, but I’d see them as coming once the core data model is dependable.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what you want the shared information storage and stable item management to accomplish.
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should act like one reliable source of truth for the user’s information, so the same item can be accessed by different compatible applications without being duplicated or drifting out of sync. When someone changes or removes an item, the system should preserve the surrounding organization as much as possible and avoid breaking related links or structures unless that change is truly necessary. In practice, I want users to feel like they can safely manage their information over time without losing what they’ve already built around it.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you describe more about what “item” types ZNIX needs to support, such as text notes, files, contacts, or other personal information objects?
turns.interviewee_utterance: I’d expect it to support a broad range of personal information objects, not just one content type. Text notes and file attachments are obvious ones, and contacts or reference records would also make sense, but I’d want the framework to stay flexible enough to handle new object types later without redesigning everything.

turns.interviewer_utterance: How should ZNIX handle different item types when it comes to storing their content and metadata, especially so new object types can be added later without redesigning the framework?
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should separate the core item container from the type-specific content, so every item has common metadata like identity, dates, tags, and relationships, while the actual payload is handled by the item type. That way, a new object type can plug in its own fields and behavior without changing how the framework stores or organizes items at the base level. I’d want the core model to stay generic enough that adding a new type feels like extension, not surgery.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What metadata fields are essential for every item in ZNIX, beyond identity, dates, tags, and relationships?
turns.interviewee_utterance: I’d say ownership or source, so you know where the item came from and which application created or last modified it, would be important. Status like active, archived, or deleted also seems useful, especially if users need to keep an organized history without losing items outright. Beyond that, I’m not sure there’s a fixed universal set; some metadata should probably be optional depending on the item type.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Are there any other stakeholders you think have valuable insights into ZNIX and whose needs should be considered?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, definitely the application developers who will integrate with ZNIX, because they’ll feel the pain points around the interface and data model first. I’d also include end users who manage a lot of personal information, since they’ll tell us whether the organization and recovery features actually feel safe and practical. If this is meant for a broader deployment, support or operations people might matter too, but I’d prioritize users and client app teams first.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What would you consider a successful deployment of ZNIX?
turns.interviewee_utterance: A successful deployment would be one where users can put their personal information into ZNIX, organize it the way they think about it, and keep using it over time without losing structure or content. It would also mean compatible applications can read and update the same data reliably, and backups or recovery work well enough that people trust the system with important information. If users feel confident that their information is safe, portable, and not locked into one app, I’d consider that a success.

turns.interviewer_utterance: To summarize, we discussed a shared information framework with stable item management, custom relationships and hierarchies, broad support for personal information object types, a generic core model with type-specific extensions, essential metadata like source and status, and a clean interface for compatible applications. Is there anything else you would like to add?
turns.interviewee_utterance: One thing I’d add is that simplicity matters a lot; the framework can be powerful, but it still needs to feel manageable for casual users. Also, I’d want the system to handle migration or evolution of item types gracefully, so people don’t lose access to older information as the framework grows. Other than that, I think the summary captures the main needs pretty well.
